title: Blaze of Glory
text: In the main rules, spellcasters are only allowed to empower spells by spending Health they have. Put another way, a spellcaster can only take his Health down to 0 to empower a spell. Under this rule, spellcasters are allowed to take their Health below 0 to empower a spell. For every point they add to their Casting Roll that would take them below 0 Health, they instead suffer a -1 on their Survival Roll after the game. For example, an apprentice attempts to cast Invisibility with a Casting Number of 12. The apprentice rolls a ‘2’. The apprentice could empower the spell by 10 to get it to successfully cast, but only has 5 Health remaining. Using Blaze of Glory, the apprentice could successfully empower the spell, using his 5 remaining Health, and then suffering -5 to his Survival Roll after the game. All other limitations to empowering a spell still apply. Remember that empowering takes place before the spell takes effect. So, the spellcaster will die and be removed from the table before the spell takes effect. Thus, there is no value in a spellcaster using this rule to empower a spell on himself (such as Heal) as the spell will have no target when it resolves. Obviously, using this rule is an extremely desperate move, and there are very few times when it will be worthwhile, but sometimes getting that last spell off is more important than personal survival.

title: Casting Roll Criticals
text: This rule makes spellcasting even more dangerous and unpredictable. Whenever spellcasters roll a natural ‘20’ on their Casting Roll, they have rolled a critical success. Conversely, if spellcasters roll a natural ‘1’ on their Casting Roll, they have rolled a critical failure. In either case, the player should look up the specific spell being cast in the Codified Spell List (see Chapter Two, page 17) to find the result of this critical. When a spellcaster rolls a critical failure, he does not take damage for failing to cast the spell. If a critical failure results in the spell being cast, treat the Casting Number as 14. Criticals are never used when a spellcaster is using a scroll, except with regard to the rules presented under Write Scroll. And, if a spellcaster is attempting to cast a spell he knows and rolls a ‘1’, he may not use a scroll even if he has one available. A spellcaster who rolls a critical failure on a Casting Roll receives +10 experience points, instead of the usual +5 for failing to cast a spell. Many of the critical results involve random distances; in all cases this cannot move a figure, or select a point, off the table. If this would be the case, stop measuring at the edge of the table and move the figure there or use that point as the randomly selected point.

title: Draining Magical Items
text: In the main rules, spellcasters are not allowed to empower Out of Game spells, although there are a few options and magical items in the expansion books that subvert this rule. (Also see Out of Game Empowering, page 13.) If this optional rule is in effect, spellcasters are allowed to empower Out of Game spells by draining the mystical force stored within magic items and weapons. Using this rule, the spellcaster may sacrifice a magical item, weapon, or armour that is stored in his vault to increase his Casting Roll by +1 for each full 100gc of the item’s sell price. For example, a wizard could sacrifice a Wand of Light (sell price 200gc) to empower an OOG spell by 2. Alternatively, the wizard could sacrifice a magic hand weapon with +1 damage (sell price 125gc) to gain +1. Only one magic item may be drained for each Casting Roll. The item is destroyed in the process and should be crossed off the Wizard Sheet. The decision to use this empowering can be made after the die is rolled. The magic within potions, scrolls, and grimoires functions differently and may not be drained in this manner. If you are also using the No Market for Created Items rule, created items may not be drained for OOG spell bonuses.

title: Flourishes
text: Over the centuries, wizards have constantly tinkered with the best-known spells, making small modifications or adding embellishments to achieve slightly different effects. These are collectively known as ‘flourishes’, and some wizards added notes in their grimoires about how to achieve them. Whenever a wizard finds or purchases a grimoire for a spell he already knows, he can use this grimoire to learn one of the flourishes listed under that spell in the Codified Spell List (see Chapter 2). This requires the wizard to spend a level in the same way as if he had learned a new spell, but there is no maximum to the number of flourishes that can be learned after each game. The wizard should make a note on his Wizard Sheet. After learning this flourish, the new grimoire is expended and should be crossed off the sheet. Flourishes can be used by wizards and apprentices but are harder to cast than the normal version of the spell. To cast a spell with a flourish, the spellcaster declares his intention and then makes his Casting Roll with the modifier listed under that flourish. If the spell succeeds, the spell is cast with the additional rules listed under that flourish. If the spell fails, the spellcaster suffers any damage as normal. The spellcaster may empower the spell following the normal rules but must empower it enough to cast the spell with the flourish (he can’t change his mind and cast the spell normally). If a spellcaster knows multiple flourishes for a given spell, he may attempt to use more than one when casting a spell; however, when attempting to cast a spell with multiple flourishes, the spellcaster suffers the modifiers of all the flourishes added together, plus an additional -1 to the Casting Roll for such a powerful magical display. Flourishes can never be cast from scrolls. If a spellcaster uses a scroll to successfully cast a spell he knows, no flourishes can be added even if he originally declared he was attempting to do so. This may prove futile if losing the flourish means the spell cannot reach or affect its intended target. Bonuses from a flourish can only be applied to each target once per game, no matter how many times a spell with a flourish is cast. Flourish cannot be taken when creating a new wizard.

title: Holding a Spell
text: If a spellcaster activates and only uses his move action (or an action that can replace a move action), and is entitled to one or more additional actions, he can instead forgo any remaining actions to ‘Hold a Spell’. Place a marker down next to the spellcaster to remember this.. At any point during the rest of the turn, directly after a member of this warband has completed an activation, the spellcaster may attempt to cast a spell, following the normal rules. This allows spellcasters to stand in readiness in case a target becomes visible later in the turn or to better sequence the spell with the movements of his warband. For example, having a soldier far away with treasure move first, before casting Leap on him. Holding a spell does come with some danger, however. If a spellcaster that is holding a spell suffers damage for any reason, his concentration is broken and he cannot cast a spell this turn (remove the marker). Also, if the warband runs out of figures to activate, such as the last soldier being killed during another player’s turn, the opportunity has also been lost.

title: No Market for Created Items
text: The wizards of modern Frostgrave only have a fraction of the knowledge and the power of the original inhabitants of Felstad. While they can make potions and enchanted items that mimic the ones found in the ruins, they are just pale imitations that will soon lose their power. For that reason, warbands are never allowed to sell items that were created by the warband – such as potions, enchanted weapons or armour, or scrolls. This applies not just to items created with spells such as Brew Potion or Embed Enchantment, but also by warband members such as the apothecary’s free healing potion. These items may be stored in the wizard’s vault but should be marked to show they cannot be sold.

title: Out of Game Empowering
text: The original reason that spellcasters were not allowed to empower spells out of game was to reduce paperwork, especially from game to game. However, this issue has changed somewhat since OOG spells were divided into Before (B) and After (A) in Second Edition. Under this optional rule, spellcasters are allowed to empower Out of Game (B) spells. In this case, the damage taken from empowering carries straight into the game about to be played. It is still not possible to empower Out of Game (A) spells.

title: Out of Game Spellcasting Limits
text: As wizards go up in level, the number of Out of Game spells they know can grow unwieldy, especially with both the wizard and apprentice attempting to cast each one before and after a game. Under this rule, each warband is limited to a maximum of four Out of Game spellcasting attempts before a game and four more after a game. These spellcasting attempts are still bound by all other rules for Out of Game spells, so the wizard and the apprentice may attempt each spell they know a maximum of once. The player is allowed to make these casting attempts sequentially, choosing which spell to attempt next after the previous roll is made. That way, if the wizard fails an OOG spell, the apprentice could attempt to cast it; but if the wizard succeeded, the wizard could attempt to cast a different spell, and so on. The limit of four is somewhat arbitrary and was chosen because it seems a decent number of rolls to make without slowing the game down too much. If players really enjoy Out of Game spells, they can increase the number of attempts allowed, but I don’t suggest going higher than six attempts.

title: Forgetting Spells
text: Most of the rules presented in this chapter can be incorporated into a Frostgrave campaign without greatly changing the inherent feel of the game. I intentionally separated this rule from the others as it is a much larger, more fundamental change to how the game is played. It also requires more careful book-keeping which might not appeal to some players. Under this rule, whenever a spellcaster fails to cast a spell, he may not use that spell again for the remainder of the game/scenario. He has temporarily forgotten it and must later consult his spell books to remember the exact words or gestures. Spellcasters may still empower their spells, and a spell successfully cast this way does not cause the spell to be forgotten. The use of a scroll, however, does. There are some large plusses to playing the game this way. It will almost certainly cause spellcasters to use a greater variety of spells as they start to forget their normal go-to spells. It encourages wizards to learn a greater variety of spells and makes the decision to empower or not more difficult. It also increases the utility of scrolls. On the downside, it does require greater book-keeping, as players must note which spells have been forgotten by the wizard and which by the apprentice (as they operate independently in this respect). It might discourage the use of flourishes, with their greater chance of failure. It could also lead to frustration, if a wizard forgets his favourite spell before he has managed to cast it once or if he managed to forget all his most useful spells early in a game. This danger is especially true early in a campaign when wizards know fewer spells and are less adept at casting them. So, players should think long and hard about incorporating this rule into the campaign. It might be worth trying out one scenario that uses this as a special rule, just to see how it works. This rule probably works best if the game is being played in a role-playing style or in longer scenarios such as dungeon crawls, where there might be quiet periods with no monsters or opposition on the table. This rule keeps spellcasters from continually casting heals and enhancements without fear of consequence (though Casting Roll Criticals also helps with that). At the end of the day, all these rules are just suggestions on potential ways to make the game more fun for you and your group. You can always try them out for a limited time and if you decide you don’t like them, drop them from the campaign.
